Nigeria’s new CBN-NNPC partnership seeks to improve petroleum revenue management, boost dollar inflows and strengthen the naira. However, production challenges, debt obligations and transparency concerns could undermine its ambitions, writes SAMI TUNJI For decades, Nigeria has faced a troubling economic contradiction. Despite being one of Africa’s largest petroleum producers and earning billions of dollars from crude oil and gas exports, the country has repeatedly struggled with foreign exchange shortages, currency depreciation and difficulties translating its natural resources into sustained economic stability. The problem extends beyond how much oil Nigeria produces or exports. Equally important is how petroleum earnings are collected, managed, converted and transferred into the financial system, particularly when businesses and investors require predictable access to foreign currency. This longstanding challenge has brought renewed attention to the relationship between the Central Bank of Nigeria and the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited, two institutions whose operations significantly influence the country’s external reserves, government revenue and foreign exchange market. On Wednesday, 18 November 2026, both institutions signed a Memorandum of Understanding at the CBN headquarters in Abuja to strengthen cooperation in managing oil and gas revenues, improving foreign exchange inflows, financing energy investments and ensuring regulatory compliance. The agreement also covers payment automation, cybersecurity, risk management and the development of financial arrangements to support the monetisation of Nigeria’s hydrocarbon resources. Although the institutions have collaborated for decades, the latest agreement establishes a more formal structure for coordinating activities that directly affect Nigeria’s foreign exchange supply. For businesses struggling with exchange rate uncertainty, the arrangement could improve the predictability of dollar inflows. For the government, it offers an opportunity to strengthen petroleum revenue management, while NNPC could benefit from improved access to financing. However, the potential gains will depend on whether the agreement addresses longstanding operational weaknesses rather than merely improving communication between both institutions. Oil revenue, naira stability The importance of the partnership becomes clearer when Nigeria’s external trade figures are examined. According to the CBN’s second-quarter 2026 economic report, Nigeria’s merchandise export earnings increased to $20.08bn from $15.56bn in the preceding quarter, representing growth of approximately 29.05 per cent. Crude oil exports contributed $9.39bn, natural gas generated $3.63bn, while refined petroleum products accounted for $3.94bn. Combined, these petroleum-related exports generated approximately $16.96bn, representing 84.46 per cent of merchandise export earnings. Non-oil exports contributed the remaining $3.12bn. The figures demonstrate Nigeria’s continued dependence on petroleum for foreign exchange, notwithstanding efforts to expand non-oil exports. However, export earnings do not automatically translate into dollars available for trading in the domestic foreign exchange market. Some receipts are retained for operational expenses, debt repayments, contractual commitments and investments. Others belong to private producers, while the timing of remittances and currency conversions can influence market liquidity. Consequently, even when export earnings increase, businesses may experience foreign exchange shortages if dollar inflows remain irregular or demand exceeds available supply. Speaking at the MoU signing, CBN Governor Olayemi Cardoso identified this challenge while explaining the significance of the agreement. “As custodian of NNPC Limited’s key operational foreign currency accounts, the Central Bank of Nigeria plays a critical role in ensuring the timely, secure and transparent settlement of oil and gas proceeds into the Federation Account and other designated government accounts,” he said. Cardoso explained that improved account management, funds transfers and liquidity support would strengthen macroeconomic stability by ensuring predictable revenue flows. “This is especially vital during periods of volatility, when dependable flows of oil revenue support monetary stability,” he added. The implications extend to manufacturers importing machinery, businesses purchasing raw materials and foreign investors seeking assurances that legitimate foreign exchange obligations can be settled. A more predictable supply of dollars could reduce uncertainty, improve financial planning and support investor confidence. The agreement comes amid improvements in Nigeria’s external position, although recent market developments indicate that vulnerabilities remain. In her remarks, the CBN Deputy Governor, Operations, Emem Usoro, disclosed that the country’s gross external reserves had exceeded $55bn, supported by higher petroleum production and sustained diaspora remittances. “Today, while our gross external reserves exceed $55bn, supported by higher oil production and sustained diaspora remittances, we are confident that this MoU will help preserve and strengthen our reserves through improved export earnings and foreign exchange inflows,” she said. Usoro explained that the arrangement would establish a transparent framework covering international trade, energy financing, liquidity support, regulatory compliance and risk management. Nevertheless, recent foreign exchange developments demonstrate why maintaining the gains could prove challenging. Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience. At the official Nigerian Foreign Exchange Market, the currency closed at N1,357.19 per dollar on 16 November, compared with N1,353.97 in the preceding trading session. The movements suggest that stronger reserves alone cannot eliminate currency volatility. Importantly, gross external reserves also differ from immediately available foreign exchange liquidity, particularly after accounting for external obligations and reserve management requirements. The CBN-NNPC agreement could therefore strengthen the reliability of petroleum-related dollar inflows, but sustained naira stability will also depend on foreign investment, remittances, import demand and broader economic conditions. Ending crisis-driven coordination The November agreement represents another stage in a relationship that has evolved considerably since Nigeria introduced major monetary and petroleum sector reforms. In February 2024, NNPC announced plans to domicile a substantial portion of its revenues and banking services with the CBN, following efforts to strengthen oversight of petroleum receipts. The arrangement was designed to improve cash management, transparency and the documentation of transactions, while allowing the company to maintain relationships with commercial banks where necessary. The latest agreement, signed approximately two years and nine months later, seeks to move beyond individual transactions towards permanent institutional coordination. Cardoso disclosed that the CBN, NNPC and other petroleum-related institutions had already been meeting approximately every two weeks to resolve operational challenges. “We are simply putting on paper what we have been discussing,” he explained. For NNPC’s Group Chief Financial Officer, Adedapo Segun, the previous approach was inadequate for the country’s economic requirements. “For too long, NNPC Limited and the CBN have cooperated on an ad hoc basis, transaction by transaction and crisis by crisis. That model will no longer serve Nigeria,” he said. Segun explained that NNPC’s transformation under the Petroleum Industry Act 2021 had increased the need for stronger financial discipline. As a commercially operated company, NNPC must manage its assets, generate returns and meet financial obligations while supporting Nigeria’s energy security. Meanwhile, the CBN must maintain monetary stability and ensure that financial transactions comply with regulatory requirements. “Energy is foreign exchange. Foreign exchange is monetary stability. Monetary stability is energy security,” Segun declared. NNPC would also align domestic payments, contractor settlements and foreign exchange conversions with CBN regulations. “This is not a ceremonial partnership. We have agreed on working groups, timelines and accountability mechanisms,” he said. According to him, NNPC Group Treasurer John Etikudo will oversee implementation on the company’s behalf, working with the CBN’s Banking Services Department. The agreement also establishes joint steering and working committees, co-chaired by both institutions, to monitor performance. Beyond improving payment efficiency, these arrangements could strengthen financial accountability by providing clearer procedures for reconciling transactions and identifying operational risks. However, their effectiveness will depend on transparent reporting and the ability to resolve disagreements without compromising either institution’s responsibilities. NNPC’s financial test The agreement also comes against the background of financial difficulties inherited by NNPC’s current management. Group Chief Executive Officer Bayo Ojulari disclosed that the company faced severe liquidity constraints, troubled projects, substantial borrowing obligations and refinery challenges when he assumed office in April 2025. “At the starting point, NNPC was in a very challenging situation. Our liquidity position was extremely weak, and the majority of our projects were heavily challenged,” he admitted. Ojulari explained that management reviewed proposed asset divestments, restructured existing loans and reconsidered additional borrowing arrangements. He acknowledged receiving guidance from Cardoso during the restructuring process. The revelations highlight the financial pressures confronting a company expected to increase petroleum production while meeting commercial obligations. The challenges are particularly significant because Nigeria’s ambition to increase crude oil production to three million barrels daily requires substantial investment. According to the Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission, Nigeria produced an average of 1.69 million barrels of crude oil and condensate daily in October 2026. This represented a 5.7 per cent increase from approximately 1.60 million barrels daily in October 2025, although production declined by 1.7 per cent from September 2026. Crude oil production alone averaged 1.51 million barrels daily, exceeding Nigeria’s 1.5-million-barrel allocation under the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries for the sixth consecutive month. The production figures reveal the scale of NNPC’s ambition. Using the October combined crude oil and condensate output of 1.69 million barrels daily, reaching three million barrels would require approximately 1.31 million additional barrels daily, representing growth of about 78 per cent. The comparison is illustrative because the three-million-barrel target must be assessed against its precise production coverage and applicable OPEC restrictions. Segun argued that stronger institutional coordination could attract the investment required to achieve the target. “That confidence is what will attract the capital Nigeria needs to grow production from 1.8 million barrels per day to three million barrels per day and unlock our vast gas resources,” he said. The financial implications could be substantial. However, additional production does not necessarily translate into equivalent increases in available dollars where petroleum earnings are committed to debt repayments or forward-sale arrangements. Cardoso said the CBN would use its institutional relationships to attract international financial institutions capable of supporting Nigeria’s natural gas development. he arrangement could help NNPC raise capital using its balance sheet and assets rather than relying exclusively on government funding. Nevertheless, the financing structures must be carefully managed to avoid transferring commercial risks to the monetary authority. For Ojulari, the agreement provides an opportunity to improve financial discipline while positioning Nigeria’s energy assets for greater competitiveness. “We are here not just for the optics. We are here to build a working partnership that delivers results,” he said. Testing outcomes Beyond the optimism expressed by both institutions, the agreement’s success will ultimately depend on measurable improvements in Nigeria’s foreign exchange market. One important indicator will be whether petroleum revenue transfers become more predictable, with fewer settlement delays and clearer reconciliation of export receipts. Another will be whether the collaboration improves NNPC’s financial management without undermining the CBN’s independence. The partnership also provides opportunities to strengthen cybersecurity, automate treasury transactions and improve the sharing of financial information. These improvements could reduce operational risks and enhance confidence in petroleum revenue management. However, closer institutional coordination cannot independently resolve Nigeria’s production constraints, eliminate exchange rate volatility or guarantee additional foreign exchange earnings. The country must also improve petroleum infrastructure, sustain investment, diversify exports and maintain credible monetary and fiscal policies. Greater transparency over NNPC’s financial obligations, including loans secured against future petroleum earnings, would help investors and the public assess how much oil revenue is available to support the economy. Regular disclosure of settlement performance, foreign exchange conversions and implementation milestones would also provide a basis for evaluating the agreement. Ultimately, the collaboration offers an opportunity to strengthen the connection between Nigeria’s petroleum wealth and monetary stability. But the distinction between managing existing earnings more efficiently and generating additional foreign exchange must remain clear. The former depends largely on institutional discipline, while the latter requires greater productive capacity, investment and stronger export performance. Cardoso observed, “When economic institutions collaborate in pursuit of a shared vision, the nation benefits, economic stability is strengthened, investor confidence rises, and the foundation for sustainable growth becomes more assured.” Whether the agreement delivers those benefits will depend on implementation, accountability and both institutions’ willingness to translate their commitments into measurable results. For Nigerians, the ultimate test will not be the agreement itself, but whether improved management of the country’s oil dollars produces a more reliable foreign exchange market, greater economic stability and stronger confidence in the naira. Sami Tunji Sami Tunji is a Senior Business Correspondent at Punch Newspapers with about five years of experience in data-driven reporting. He covers finance, ICT, and broader macroeconomic issues, combining analytical insight with clear storytelling. Sami’s work reflects strong editorial judgment, professional development, and a commitment to accurate and informative business journalism.
